q: In activity-based costing, a 'duration driver' differs from a 'transaction driver' in that a duration driver:

options.A: Counts how many times an activity is performed, ignoring how long it takes on each occasion
options.B: Measures the amount of time required each time the activity is performed, and is used where the time taken varies significantly between occurrences
options.C: Is used only for facility-sustaining activities of the enterprise
options.D: Allocates the cost of an activity in proportion to the sales value of the output produced

q: The first stage of the two-stage allocation procedure in activity-based costing consists of:

options.A: Assigning the costs accumulated in activity cost pools to products with the help of cost drivers
options.B: Tracing all direct costs to the cost objects that caused them
options.C: Charging the overheads of the whole plant to products on a single plant-wide rate
options.D: Assigning the costs of the resources consumed to the activities that consume them, thereby forming activity cost pools

q: A factory's order-processing cost pool is Rs 6,00,000 for a period in which 2,000 purchase orders were processed. Product P, for which 450 purchase orders were placed, will be assigned order-processing cost of:
A cost pool in activity-based costing is regarded as homogeneous when:

options.A: It contains only costs that are fixed in nature
options.B: All the costs collected in it relate to one single department
options.C: All the costs in it are driven by one and the same cost driver, so that a single driver rate adequately explains the whole pool
options.D: The total of the pool is small in relation to the total overheads

q: Activity-based costing draws attention to the cost of unused (idle) capacity mainly because:

options.A: Activity rates are worked out on the practical capacity of the activity, so the cost of capacity supplied but not used is reported separately instead of being loaded on to the products made
options.B: It treats the whole cost of idle capacity as a direct cost of the products
options.C: It writes off the cost of idle capacity to the Profit and Loss Account without reporting it to management
options.D: It assumes that every activity always works at its theoretical maximum capacity

q: Traditional volume-based costing is said to produce 'cross-subsidisation' between products because:

options.A: The selling prices of all products are kept uniform by the costing system
options.B: Direct costs are traced to the wrong products under the traditional system
options.C: Products are subsidised by the government in proportion to their volume
options.D: High-volume products absorb overheads in proportion to volume and so carry part of the costs actually caused by low-volume, complex products, which are consequently under-costed

q: A plant's overheads of Rs 12,00,000 consist of set-up costs Rs 5,00,000 (500 set-ups), inspection costs Rs 4,00,000 (2,000 inspections) and machining costs Rs 3,00,000 (30,000 machine hours). Product X uses 40 set-ups, 300 inspections and 4,000 machine hours. The overhead assigned to Product X under activity-based costing is:
Activity-based costing can be applied in a bank or a hospital, although they produce no physical product, because:

options.A: Such organisations incur no indirect costs at all
options.B: Their costs are likewise caused by activities performed, and their services, customers or patients can be treated as cost objects to which activity costs are assigned through cost drivers
options.C: Their entire expenditure is recovered from the government
options.D: The activities of a service organisation need not be identified before costs are assigned

q: In selecting a cost driver for an activity cost pool, the consideration that should dominate is:

options.A: Whether a cause-and-effect relationship exists between changes in the driver and changes in the cost of the activity
options.B: Whether the driver is the easiest of all to count, whatever its relation to the cost
options.C: Whether the driver was also used in the previous accounting period
options.D: Whether the driver is expressed in rupees rather than in physical units

q: A recognised limitation of activity-based costing is that:

options.A: It cannot be used where a factory makes more than one product
options.B: It always shows every product to be more costly than absorption costing does
options.C: It requires the enterprise to abandon the recording of direct costs
options.D: It is costly and time-consuming to identify activities, measure the drivers and keep the system up to date, and some assignments, such as those of facility-sustaining costs, still rest on arbitrary bases

q: A task follows an 80% learning curve and the first unit takes 100 hours. The cumulative average time per unit after 8 units have been produced is:

options.A: 80 hours
options.B: 51.2 hours
options.C: 64 hours
options.D: 40.96 hours

q: The learning curve effect on labour time is expected to taper off and reach a steady state mainly because:

options.A: Workers deliberately slow down once they have mastered a task
options.B: The learning percentage changes automatically after every doubling of output
options.C: As cumulative output grows, the workers approach a limit set by the process and the equipment, beyond which repetition yields little further reduction in the time taken
options.D: Supervisors stop recording the time taken after the initial units

q: Knowledge of the learning rate applicable to a new product is most directly useful to management in:

options.A: Estimating the labour cost of a large order at the tendering stage, and in preparing production schedules and labour budgets that fall as the cumulative volume rises
options.B: Fixing the useful life of the plant used on the product
options.C: Deciding the depreciation method to be applied to the equipment
options.D: Valuing the closing stock of raw materials of the factory

q: The incremental unit-time model of the learning curve differs from the cumulative average-time model in that the incremental model:

options.A: Assumes that no learning takes place after the first unit
options.B: Applies the learning percentage to the total time of all the units produced
options.C: Expresses learning in terms of material cost instead of labour time
options.D: Applies the learning percentage to the time taken by the last unit produced, rather than to the average time per unit over all the units produced so far

q: The first unit of a job takes 50 hours and the job follows a 90% learning curve. The cumulative average time per unit when 4 units have been completed is:

options.A: 45 hours
options.B: 36.45 hours
options.C: 40.5 hours
options.D: 50 hours

q: In target costing, the 'drifting cost' of a proposed product means:

options.A: The cost at which the product would come out if it were designed and produced with the firm's present capabilities and methods, before any deliberate cost-reduction effort is applied
options.B: The target cost itself, after it has been approved by management
options.C: The amount by which the actual cost drifts above the standard cost during production
options.D: The cost of the product after all kaizen improvements have been exhausted

q: The cost gap in target costing is closed principally by:

options.A: Raising the selling price above the price the market will bear
options.B: Reducing the profit margin required by the enterprise
options.C: Transferring a part of the cost to the overheads of other products
options.D: Value engineering and redesign of the product and its processes during the design stage, carried out in cooperation with the suppliers concerned

q: Target costing compels attention to the customer and the market at the design stage because:

options.A: The selling price is fixed by adding the desired margin to the estimated cost
options.B: The allowable cost is derived from the price customers are willing to pay, so features that customers do not value enough to pay for cannot be allowed to add to the cost
options.C: Customers participate directly in preparing the cost estimates of the firm
options.D: The design stage is the only stage at which market research can be conducted

q: A company will launch a product for which customers will pay no more than Rs 1,600 per unit, and it requires a profit margin of 20% on the selling price. The allowable (target) cost per unit is:
Under kaizen costing, cost reduction during the production stage is pursued chiefly through:

options.A: Many small, continuous improvements in the existing processes, made by the workers and supervisors who themselves operate those processes
options.B: A complete redesign of the product before production begins
options.C: Replacing the entire workforce with automated equipment at one stroke
options.D: Renegotiating the selling price of the product with customers

q: 'Kaikaku', as a means of improvement, differs from 'kaizen' in that kaikaku refers to:

options.A: The routine maintenance of machines by their operators
options.B: Improvement obtained by working longer hours on the same process
options.C: The transfer of a process to another factory of the same enterprise
options.D: A radical, large-scale redesign of a process that produces a dramatic improvement at one stroke, as against the gradual, incremental gains of kaizen

q: In a kaizen costing system, the failure of a work team to achieve a periodic cost-reduction target is treated primarily as:

options.A: Grounds for imposing a monetary penalty on the members of the team
options.B: A signal to analyse the process and support the team in removing the obstacles to improvement, since the target presupposes that the process itself must keep improving and not merely that the workers must exert themselves more
options.C: Proof that kaizen costing should be abandoned in favour of standard costing
options.D: A variance to be written off without any investigation

q: A firm's quality costs for a year are: prevention Rs 1,50,000, appraisal Rs 2,50,000, internal failure Rs 3,00,000 and external failure Rs 2,00,000. Its total cost of quality for the year is:
Expenditure on reworking defective units detected before despatch, and on material scrapped because of defective production, is classified in a cost of quality report as:

options.A: Prevention cost
options.B: Appraisal cost
options.C: Internal failure cost
options.D: External failure cost

q: Warranty claims settled, product-liability costs and the cost of handling goods returned by customers as defective are classified in a cost of quality report as:

options.A: External failure costs
options.B: Internal failure costs
options.C: Appraisal costs
options.D: Prevention costs

q: The 'hidden' costs of poor quality, which a conventional cost of quality report often fails to capture, include:

options.A: The cost of calibrating inspection equipment
options.B: Lost sales and loss of goodwill arising from dissatisfied customers, which do not pass through the accounts as identifiable quality costs
options.C: The salaries of the quality inspection staff
options.D: The cost of training workers in quality methods

q: A product sells for Rs 850 per unit, its totally variable (material) cost is Rs 340 per unit, and each unit occupies the bottleneck machine for 0.5 hour. The return per factory hour of the product is:

options.A: Rs 510
options.D: Rs 255

q: In the Theory of Constraints, the step of 'subordinating' all other operations to the constraint means:

options.A: Reducing the capacity of the bottleneck resource to the level of the other resources
options.B: Keeping every non-bottleneck resource fully busy, whether or not its output is needed
options.C: Stopping all operations other than the bottleneck operation
options.D: Scheduling the non-bottleneck resources so that they support the maximum output of the bottleneck, even if they themselves remain idle at times, instead of being kept busy producing unwanted work-in-progress

q: If, after the constraint has been fully exploited and all other operations subordinated to it, the capacity of the bottleneck still falls short of the market demand, the next step in the Theory of Constraints is to:

options.A: Abandon the product that uses the bottleneck resource
options.B: Reduce the selling prices so that the demand falls to the level of the capacity
options.C: 'Elevate' the constraint, that is, spend to increase its capacity, for example through overtime, an additional machine or off-loading of work, and then return to identify the new constraint
options.D: Build up a large stock of finished goods ahead of the bottleneck

q: Because throughput accounting values inventory at material cost only, it discourages production merely for building up stock, in that:

options.A: Producing units that are not sold adds nothing to throughput or to profit, since labour and overheads are charged as operating expenses of the period in which they are incurred
options.B: Unsold units are valued at full absorption cost under throughput accounting
options.C: Material cost is excluded altogether from the value of inventory
options.D: Stock once produced can never be sold in a later period

q: Under backflush costing, 10,000 units are completed in a period. The standard cost is Rs 45 per unit for materials and Rs 30 per unit for conversion. On completion, the amount debited to the finished goods account is:
Backflush costing is so named because, in a just-in-time environment, the cost accounting entries are:

options.A: Made in advance, at the beginning of the period, for the whole period's expected production
options.B: Delayed until a trigger point, such as the completion of finished output or its sale, at which point costs are flushed back and assigned to the units produced at standard cost
options.C: Omitted altogether, no cost records being maintained under the system
options.D: Posted separately for every operation through which each unit passes

q: In a just-in-time pull system, production at a workstation is authorised by:

options.A: The monthly production schedule issued by the head office, regardless of the actual demand
options.B: A signal (kanban) from the succeeding workstation indicating that it has consumed material and needs replenishment, so that nothing is made merely to keep the workstation busy
options.C: The availability of idle labour at the workstation
options.D: The need to utilise the full rated capacity of every machine

q: Successful working of just-in-time purchasing depends most critically on:

options.A: A small number of reliable suppliers delivering small quantities frequently, to certified quality, so that incoming inspection and buffer stocks can largely be dispensed with
options.B: Maintaining several months' stock of every purchased item as a safeguard
options.C: Buying always from the supplier quoting the lowest price, whatever the reliability of delivery
options.D: Placing one large order a year covering the entire annual requirement

q: The estimated life-cycle costs of a product are: research and development Rs 30,00,000, launch and marketing Rs 5,00,000, production of 10,000 units at Rs 400 per unit, after-sales service Rs 3,00,000 and disposal Rs 2,00,000. The life-cycle cost per unit is:

options.A: Rs 750
options.B: Rs 800
options.C: Rs 400

q: From the producer's viewpoint, product life-cycle costing requires the costs of a product to be accumulated and reported:

options.A: By the calendar years in which the cash is paid out
options.B: Only up to the point at which the product is first sold
options.C: By each phase of the product's life, from development through introduction, growth, maturity and decline to withdrawal, rather than by accounting years alone
options.D: By the departments of the factory through which the product passes

q: A component's value index (worth divided by cost) works out to 0.6. The correct interpretation is:

options.A: The component shows excellent value and needs no study
options.B: The function is being performed at less than its worth, which is not possible
options.C: The value index has no bearing on the selection of items for study
options.D: The function is being obtained at a cost well above its worth, which marks the component out as a prime candidate for value engineering

q: In value analysis, a 'secondary function' of a component is one which:

options.A: Is the essential purpose for which the component exists
options.B: Supports or assists the basic function, or arises from the particular design chosen, rather than being the basic purpose of the component
options.C: Is performed by the component only after it has failed in service
options.D: Cannot be described in words at all

q: The current cost of a product is Rs 625 per unit. Under kaizen costing, a cost-reduction rate of 8% is set for the next period. The kaizen target cost per unit for that period is:

options.A: Rs 633
options.B: Rs 617
options.C: Rs 600
options.D: Rs 575

q: Under the Total Quality Management view of quality costs, the optimum level of quality is approached by:

options.A: Driving defects towards zero through prevention, on the view that the cost of prevention rises by less than the failure costs it eliminates, so that the total quality cost falls as conformance improves
options.B: Inspecting every unit twice so that no defective unit can reach a customer
options.C: Accepting a fixed percentage of defective output as economically unavoidable in all circumstances
options.D: Spending nothing on prevention and meeting failure costs as and when they arise

q: A cost of quality report serves management control principally by:

options.A: Fixing responsibility for every defective unit on the worker who produced it
options.B: Showing the inspection department how many units it examined during the period
options.C: Showing the size of the quality costs and their distribution among prevention, appraisal and failure categories, thereby directing attention and resources to where quality spending will reduce the total cost the most
options.D: Replacing the profit and loss account of the enterprise for the period

q: Under activity-based costing, a customer-service cost pool of Rs 7,20,000 is driven by the number of service calls, which total 3,600 in the period. A customer segment accounting for 850 service calls will be assigned customer-service cost of:
A recognised vulnerability of a just-in-time system operated with virtually no buffer stocks is that:

options.A: The quality of the output invariably deteriorates under the system
options.B: Workers cannot be trained to operate more than one machine
options.C: The system can work only in very small factories
options.D: Any disruption, such as a supplier failure, a breakdown or a transport stoppage, can halt the whole production line quickly, since there is no inventory cushion to fall back upon

q: The present cost of performing a function is Rs 2,40,000 and the worth of the function, that is, the lowest cost of performing it reliably by an alternative, is Rs 1,80,000. The value index of the function is:
A limitation to be kept in view when applying the learning curve to cost estimates is that:

options.A: Learning takes place only in the first unit of a job and never thereafter
options.B: The curve can be applied only to material costs and never to labour
options.C: The assumed learning rate may not hold where the work is machine-paced, the workforce or the methods change, or production is interrupted, so that estimates based on it can mislead
options.D: The cumulative output of a job can never be doubled in practice

q: A cost which will be borne in exactly the same amount whichever of the alternatives under consideration is finally chosen is, for the purpose of that decision:

options.A: A relevant cost, because it forms part of the total cost of each alternative
options.B: An irrelevant cost, to be left out of the comparison because it cannot affect the choice
options.C: An opportunity cost, because one alternative must be given up for the other
options.D: A sunk cost, because it has already been incurred in the past

q: A company is deciding whether to launch a new product. It has already spent Rs 8,50,000 on research and on a market survey for this very product. In the launch decision, this expenditure is:

options.A: A relevant cost, to be recovered out of the price of the new product
options.B: An opportunity cost of launching the product
options.C: A sunk cost, to be ignored because it will remain the same whether the product is launched or not
options.D: A differential cost between launching and not launching

q: An old machine, whose book value in the accounts is Rs 2,20,000, can be sold at once for Rs 75,000 if a proposed replacement is carried out. In evaluating the replacement proposal, the figure relevant to the decision in respect of the old machine is:

options.A: Rs 75,000, being the disposal proceeds forgone if the machine is retained
options.B: Rs 2,20,000, being the book value written in the accounts
options.C: Rs 1,45,000, being the loss that would arise on its disposal
options.D: Nil, because the machine has already been paid for in an earlier year

q: A factory has 12,000 machine hours available. Product P gives a contribution of Rs 96 per unit, takes 4 machine hours per unit and has a maximum demand of 2,200 units. Product Q gives a contribution of Rs 65 per unit and takes 5 machine hours per unit. After meeting the full demand for the product ranking first on contribution per machine hour, the number of units of Q that can be produced is:

options.A: 760 units
options.B: 600 units
options.C: 800 units
options.D: 640 units

q: A machine in a factory is lying idle and the spare time on it has no other work to which it can be put. The opportunity cost of using this spare time on a proposed job is:

options.A: Nil, because the idle time has no alternative use to be given up
options.B: The normal machine hour rate charged in the cost accounts
options.C: The depreciation of the machine for the period of the job
options.D: The contribution earned by the machine in the previous year

q: A part can be made in the factory at a variable cost of Rs 58 per unit or bought from outside at Rs 64 per unit. If the part is bought, the capacity so released can be employed on other work yielding a contribution of Rs 9 per unit of the part not made. The correct decision is to:

options.A: Make the part, because its variable cost of Rs 58 is below the purchase price of Rs 64
options.B: Buy the part, because its effective cost of Rs 55 (Rs 64 minus Rs 9) is below the variable cost of making it
options.C: Make the part, because outside supplies cannot be relied upon for quality
options.D: Remain indifferent, because the two courses differ by only Re 1 per unit

q: A special job can be completed within normal working hours by workmen who are paid a monthly salary and who would otherwise remain idle, no other work being displaced. The incremental labour cost of the job is:

options.A: The monthly salary of the workmen apportioned to the hours spent on the job
options.B: The standard labour cost of the job at normal wage rates
options.C: The overtime premium payable for the hours spent on the job
options.D: Nil, because the salaries will be paid in any case and no extra payment arises

q: A firm with spare capacity receives a one-time order for 8,000 units at Rs 92 per unit. The variable cost is Rs 78 per unit and accepting the order will require additional fixed expenditure of Rs 64,000, regular sales remaining unaffected. The order should be:

options.A: Rejected, because the additional fixed expenditure wipes out the whole gain
options.B: Accepted only if the price is raised so as to cover the full cost per unit
options.C: Accepted, because it yields a net incremental gain of Rs 48,000
options.D: Rejected, because the price is below the normal selling price of the product

q: The salary of the general manager and the rent of the head office are apportioned to a product line in the cost accounts. In deciding whether that line should be dropped, these apportioned amounts are:

options.A: Irrelevant, because they will continue in total even if the line is dropped
options.B: Relevant, because every product must bear its full share of the costs of the business
options.C: Relevant only to the extent of one-half of the amount apportioned
options.D: To be treated as the avoidable fixed costs of the line

q: The shadow price of a limiting factor, as used in short-term product-mix decisions, represents:

options.A: The market price at which the scarce resource can be sold in its raw state
options.B: The standard cost at which the resource is charged to production
options.C: The depreciation charge attaching to the machine that constitutes the bottleneck
options.D: The maximum extra amount worth paying for one more unit of the scarce resource, measured by the contribution it would earn in its best use

q: The fixed costs of a plant total Rs 6,80,000 a year. Of these, Rs 2,60,000 will still have to be borne if operations are suspended, and suspension itself will entail closure costs of Rs 30,000. Each unit sold contributes Rs 45. The shut-down point of the plant is:

options.A: 6,000 units
options.B: 8,667 units
options.C: 15,111 units
options.D: 9,333 units

q: In deciding whether a joint product should be sold at the split-off point or processed further, the share of the joint cost apportioned to that product is:

options.A: Relevant, because it forms part of the cost of the product at the split-off point
options.B: Relevant only where the apportionment is made on the sales value basis
options.C: Irrelevant, because it is a past, common cost that will be incurred in the same amount under either course
options.D: To be added to the further processing cost before the comparison is made

q: A manufacturer is able to quote a distinctly lower price for an export order than for home sales and still gain from the order, chiefly because:

options.A: Export sales are exempt from all variable costs of production
options.B: The fixed costs of the factory are already recovered from the home market, so the export order need only cover its incremental cost where spare capacity exists
options.C: Foreign buyers invariably pay in advance, removing all cost of finance
options.D: The full cost of the export units is transferred to the home customers

q: A product line shows sales of Rs 9,50,000, variable costs of Rs 6,65,000 and fixed costs of Rs 3,10,000 that are specific to the line and would be saved if it were dropped; a further Rs 1,80,000 of common fixed costs is apportioned to it. If the line is dropped, the total profit of the business will:

options.A: Fall by Rs 25,000
options.B: Fall by Rs 2,05,000
options.C: Remain unchanged
options.D: Rise by Rs 25,000

q: A plant is closed for a slack season with the intention of reopening it when demand revives. As distinct from a permanent closure, the temporary shut-down decision must additionally weigh:

options.A: Only the book value of the plant and machinery installed in it
options.B: The costs of mothballing and restarting the plant and of retaining or re-engaging the key staff needed on reopening
options.C: The total historical cost incurred in setting up the plant
options.D: The profit earned by the plant in the last normal year

q: A joint product can be sold at the split-off point for Rs 110 per unit. It can instead be processed further at a separable cost of Rs 34 per unit and then sold for Rs 152 per unit. The correct course is to:

options.A: Process it further, gaining Rs 8 per unit, since the extra revenue of Rs 42 exceeds the separable cost of Rs 34
options.B: Sell it at the split-off point, because the further processing cost must also bear a share of the joint cost
options.C: Sell it at the split-off point, gaining Rs 110 per unit without any further outlay
options.D: Process it further only if the joint cost apportioned to it is less than Rs 8 per unit

q: A job requires a material which is in short supply and cannot be replenished at present. Every kilogram used on this job will curtail the output of another regular product. The relevant cost of the material for this job is measured by:

options.A: Its original purchase price recorded in the stores ledger
options.B: Its current market price, whether or not supplies can actually be obtained
options.C: The contribution that will be forgone on the regular product whose output is curtailed
options.D: Nil, because the material is already available within the factory

q: Skilled labour hours are the limiting factor in a factory. Product A gives a contribution of Rs 132 per unit and requires 6 labour hours per unit; Product B gives a contribution of Rs 147 per unit and requires 7 labour hours per unit; Product C gives a contribution of Rs 95 per unit and requires 5 labour hours per unit. First production priority should be given to:

options.A: Product B, because its contribution per unit is the highest of the three
options.B: Product A, because its contribution per labour hour of Rs 22 is the highest of the three
options.C: Product C, because it takes the fewest labour hours per unit
options.D: All three products in proportion to their maximum demand

q: Where the factor that limits a business is the total sales value that the market can absorb, and each product competes for that limited sales value, the products should be ranked for preference according to:

options.A: Contribution per unit of the product
options.B: Net profit per unit after all overheads are absorbed
options.C: Gross profit per unit of the product
options.D: The P/V ratio, that is, the contribution earned per rupee of sales value

q: A component is used in the factory at the rate of one per finished unit. Making it in the factory involves direct material of Rs 70, direct labour of Rs 34 and variable overheads of Rs 20 per unit. A supplier offers the component at Rs 138 per unit. Allocated fixed overheads of Rs 16 per unit will continue whether the component is made or bought, and the capacity concerned has no other use. The correct decision is to:

options.A: Make the component, saving Rs 14 per unit against the supplier's price
options.B: Buy the component, because its total in-house cost of Rs 140 exceeds the price of Rs 138
options.C: Buy the component, because the fixed overheads of Rs 16 will then be saved
options.D: Remain indifferent, because making and buying cost the same in total

q: A supplier's price for a component is lower than the relevant cost of making it, yet the firm continues to make the component itself because its design is a closely guarded secret and a failure of the component would destroy the reputation of the finished product. This continuance rests on:

options.A: The sunk cost already spent on the plant used for the component
options.B: The full absorbed cost of the component shown in the cost accounts
options.C: Qualitative considerations — protection of the design secret and assurance of quality — which the cost comparison alone does not capture
options.D: The book value of the special plant installed for making the component

q: A factory is working at full capacity. Its regular selling price is Rs 240 per unit and the variable cost is Rs 150 per unit. An export order can be executed only by displacing an equal number of regular home sales. The lowest price per unit at which the export order can be accepted without loss is:

options.A: Rs 150
options.B: Rs 240
options.C: Rs 195
options.D: Rs 90

q: A firm is judging a proposal to add an entirely new product to its range. The costs properly to be charged against the proposal in the appraisal include:

options.A: A share of the existing head-office expenses apportioned on the basis of sales
options.B: The whole of the fixed costs of the factory, since the new product will use the factory
options.C: The depreciation of the existing plant which the new product will share
options.D: The additional fixed costs that will be incurred only if the product is added, such as the salary of a supervisor engaged specially for it

q: A factory has 26,000 kg of a scarce material. Product A gives a contribution of Rs 180 per unit, uses 5 kg per unit and has a maximum demand of 3,200 units. Product B gives a contribution of Rs 126 per unit, uses 3 kg per unit and has a maximum demand of 4,000 units. The maximum total contribution obtainable from the material is:
Several customer orders compete for the time of one bottleneck machine in a jobbing factory. To maximise the profit from the available machine time, the orders should be taken up in the order of:

options.A: The total contract value of each order, highest first
options.B: The contribution per unit of the article ordered
options.C: The contribution earned per hour of bottleneck machine time occupied by the order
options.D: The date on which each order was received, earliest first

q: Under a lease already signed, a firm must pay rent of Rs 60,000 a month for the next three years whether the premises are used fully, partly or not at all. In a short-term choice among products, all of which would be housed in these same premises, this rent is:

options.A: A relevant cost of the product occupying the largest floor area
options.B: A committed cost, locked in by the earlier signing of the lease and unalterable by the present choice, hence to be left out of the comparison
options.C: An opportunity cost of every product made in the premises
options.D: A sunk cost, because the lease was signed in a past period

q: A one-time order is received for 2,400 units. The variable cost is Rs 56 per unit and a set-up cost of Rs 19,200, which has no other purpose, must be incurred to execute the order. Spare capacity exists and no regular sale will be lost. The lowest price per unit at which the order can be accepted without loss is:

options.A: Rs 56
options.B: Rs 60
options.C: Rs 64
options.D: Rs 72

q: A firm proposes to drop one product and to use the machine time so released for another product already in its range. The sound way to judge the proposal is to compare:

options.A: The reported profit of the product to be dropped with the reported profit of the other product
options.B: The sales values of the two products at their present volumes
options.C: The full absorbed cost per unit of the two products
options.D: The total contribution of the whole product mix before the change with the total contribution of the whole mix after it

q: In the coming slack season a plant expects to sell only 7,500 units, each contributing Rs 52. Its avoidable fixed costs are Rs 4,30,000, its unavoidable fixed costs are Rs 1,90,000, and closing the plant for the season would itself cost Rs 25,000. For that season, the plant should:

options.A: Continue operating, because shutting down would increase the loss by Rs 15,000
options.B: Continue operating, because the expected sales give it a positive segment margin
options.C: Shut down, because the loss of Rs 2,15,000 on shutting down is smaller than the loss of Rs 2,30,000 on continuing
options.D: Shut down, because on closure the whole of its fixed costs will be saved

q: In a factory where one machine is the bottleneck governing the output of the whole plant, sound scheduling of the product mix requires that:

options.A: Every machine in the plant is kept running for the same number of hours
options.B: The bottleneck machine is loaded only after all other machines have been fully loaded
options.C: Output is stored ahead of the bottleneck so that it is never starved of material from outside
options.D: The bottleneck machine is kept fully occupied on the most rewarding work, even if this leaves some non-bottleneck machines idle for part of the time

q: A joint product has an output of 6,000 units. It can be sold at the split-off point for Rs 38 per unit, or processed further at a separable cost of Rs 14 per unit and sold for Rs 57 per unit. Processing it further will increase the total profit by:

options.D: Rs 5

q: A job is to be priced using a material which the firm consumes continuously in its regular production and replaces as it is used. The units to be drawn from stock were purchased earlier at a lower price. The cost properly to be charged to the job for this material is:

options.A: The current replacement price, because consuming the stock obliges the firm to replace it at that price
options.B: The older purchase price recorded in the stores ledger for those units
options.C: Nil, because the material is already lying in the stores
options.D: The average of the old purchase price and the current replacement price

q: A firm proposes to house a new product line in a building owned by it, which is at present let out at a rent of Rs 45,000 per month. The amount to be reckoned as the annual cost of accommodation in appraising the new line is:

options.A: Nil, because the firm owns the building and pays no rent for it
options.B: The municipal taxes and insurance of the building for the year
options.C: The depreciation of the building for the year
options.D: Rs 5,40,000, being the rent that will be forgone by withdrawing the building from letting

q: Apart from the figures of cost, the principal risk in accepting a one-time order at a price well below the normal price, even where the order itself shows an incremental gain, is that:

options.A: The variable cost per unit of regular production will necessarily rise
options.B: The fixed costs of the factory will increase in the following year
options.C: Regular customers may come to know of the lower price and press for the same terms, undermining the normal price structure
options.D: The order will have to be shown separately in the published accounts of the firm

q: A firm shifts 2,000 machine hours from a product earning a contribution of Rs 18 per machine hour to another product earning a contribution of Rs 26 per machine hour, the total machine hours and the fixed costs remaining unchanged. As a result, the total profit of the firm will:

options.A: Rise by Rs 16,000
options.B: Rise by Rs 52,000
options.C: Rise by Rs 8,000
options.D: Remain unchanged, because the total hours worked are the same

q: The rent of premises taken on lease exclusively for one product line is wholly traceable to that line, but two years of the lease still remain and the rent must be paid for that period in any event. For a decision taken now on dropping the line, the correct treatment is that:

options.A: Traceability and avoidability are different tests: a cost may be wholly traceable to a segment and yet be unavoidable within the period covered by the decision
options.B: Every traceable cost of a segment is automatically an avoidable cost of that segment
options.C: The rent should be treated as a sunk cost because the premises were taken in an earlier year
options.D: The rent should be ignored altogether because it is a fixed cost

q: A special job needs 1 kg of a material already in stock for every unit made. The material was bought at Rs 64 per kg, it has no other use in the factory, and it could be sold off as scrap for Rs 19 per kg. The relevant cost of the material per unit of the job is:

options.A: Rs 64
options.B: Rs 45
options.C: Nil
options.D: Rs 19

q: When the output of a factory is restricted by two scarce factors operating together, such as machine hours and a rationed material, the product mix giving the maximum total contribution is found by applying:

options.A: The P/V ratio ranking of the products taken one at a time
options.B: The contribution per unit ranking applied to the first factor only
options.C: Linear programming, which works out the combination of products that satisfies both restrictions together at the highest total contribution
options.D: The full-cost profit per unit of each product

q: Relevant-cost reasoning, which justifies accepting work at any price above incremental cost, is a short-run guide only, because in the long run:

options.A: Variable costs cease to be incurred altogether
options.B: Prices must in total cover all the costs of the business, including its fixed costs, if the business is to survive and replace its assets
options.C: Fixed costs become irrelevant to every decision of the business
options.D: Opportunity costs no longer arise on any resource

q: A joint product can be processed further only by hiring an additional facility, to be used for no other purpose, at a rent of Rs 90,000 for the season. In the sell-or-process-further comparison, this rent is:

options.A: A relevant cost of processing further, because it will be incurred only if that course is adopted
options.B: A joint cost, to be apportioned between the products before the comparison
options.C: Irrelevant, because it is a fixed cost and fixed costs never enter such decisions
options.D: To be charged against the option of selling at the split-off point

q: Accepting a rush order will delay the execution of work already promised to regular customers, and the firm will become liable to pay damages of Rs 40,000 for that delay. In judging the rush order, this amount is:

options.A: A general overhead of the factory, to be spread over all the work of the period
options.B: Irrelevant, because it arises under contracts with other customers
options.C: A sunk cost, because the promises to the regular customers were made earlier
options.D: A relevant cost of the rush order, because it will be incurred only if the order is accepted

q: A product earns only a small contribution of its own, but its presence in the range brings customers who also buy other, highly profitable products of the firm. Before dropping this product on the strength of its own figures, the firm must also reckon:

options.A: The book value of the plant employed on the product
options.B: The fall in the contribution of the other products that its withdrawal is likely to cause
options.C: The share of head-office costs at present apportioned to the product
options.D: The profit reported on the product in the previous year

q: If a component is bought from outside instead of being made, a special machine used solely for making it can be sold at once for Rs 1,35,000. In the make-or-buy comparison, this amount is:

options.A: A sunk receipt, to be ignored because the machine was bought in an earlier year
options.B: A part of the purchase price payable to the outside supplier
options.C: A relevant benefit of the buying alternative, to be set against the cost of buying
options.D: To be deducted from the book value of the machine before any comparison is made

q: In a business whose growth is held back by a shortage of working capital, so that finance itself is the limiting factor, competing products should be ranked for the use of the available funds according to:

options.A: The contribution earned per rupee of working capital that each product ties up
options.B: The selling price per unit of each product
options.C: The net profit per unit after absorbing all overheads
options.D: The number of units of each product that can be sold in the market

q: In every short-term decision of the kind dealt with by relevant costing — making or buying, dropping or retaining a line, accepting or refusing an order — the course to be preferred is the one which:

options.A: Shows the highest profit after all fixed and common costs have been fully absorbed
options.B: Employs the largest share of the capacity of the factory
options.C: Gives the highest incremental profit, that is, the greatest excess of incremental revenue over incremental cost, opportunity costs included
options.D: Recovers the sunk costs that have already been incurred on the product concerned

q: In the risk-adjusted discount rate method of appraising a risky project, the risk is taken into account by:

options.A: Reducing each expected cash inflow by a fixed percentage before discounting
options.B: Discounting the expected cash flows at a rate higher than the risk-free rate, the excess being a risk premium
options.C: Discounting the cash flows at the risk-free rate and then deducting a lump-sum risk allowance from the present value
options.D: Shortening the payback requirement imposed on the project

q: The essential difference between the risk-adjusted discount rate method and the certainty-equivalent method is that:

options.A: The former uses expected values of cash flows while the latter uses the most likely values
options.B: The former can be used only for replacement decisions while the latter is confined to expansion projects
options.C: The former adjusts the discount rate (the denominator), while the latter adjusts the cash flows themselves (the numerator) and then discounts at the risk-free rate
options.D: The former ignores the time value of money while the latter recognises it

q: The expected cash inflow of a project in Year 1 is Rs 2,00,000 and its certainty-equivalent coefficient for that year is 0.80. The risk-free rate is 10 per cent, the present value factor for Year 1 at 10 per cent being 0.909. The present value of the Year 1 inflow under the certainty-equivalent method is:

Two projects are identical in size, life and expected cash flows, but one of them is judged to be considerably more risky than the other. Under the risk-adjusted discount rate method, the riskier project should be appraised by:

options.A: Using the same discount rate for both, since the expected flows are identical
options.B: Using a lower discount rate, so that its present value is not understated
options.C: Using the risk-free rate, risk being dealt with separately through the payback test
options.D: Using a higher discount rate than the one applied to the less risky project

q: A project costing Rs 10,00,000 is expected to yield cash inflows of Rs 6,05,000 at the end of Year 1 and Rs 7,26,000 at the end of Year 2. Its risk-adjusted discount rate is 10 per cent. Its net present value at that rate is:
The certainty-equivalent coefficient (alpha) for a particular year's cash flow is defined as the ratio of:

options.A: The certain cash flow the decision-maker would accept in exchange for the risky expected flow, to that risky expected flow
options.B: The risky expected cash flow to the certain cash flow accepted in exchange for it
options.C: The standard deviation of the cash flow to its expected value
options.D: The present value of the cash flow to its future value

q: A manager is indifferent between receiving a certain Rs 72,000 and the prospect of receiving an expected but risky Rs 90,000 in the same year. The certainty-equivalent coefficient for that year's cash flow is:
A recognised weakness of applying a single risk-adjusted discount rate to all the years of a long-lived project is that:

options.A: It cannot be applied where the cash flows are uneven
options.B: It requires probability estimates for every year, which are rarely available
options.C: It gives a higher present value to distant cash flows than to near ones
options.D: Discounting at the raised rate compounds the risk allowance year after year, so risk is implicitly assumed to grow with time at a constant rate

q: An advantage claimed for the certainty-equivalent method over the risk-adjusted discount rate method is that it:

options.A: Dispenses altogether with the need for any subjective judgement about risk
options.B: Separates the adjustment for risk from the adjustment for the time value of money, instead of combining both in a single raised rate
options.C: Always produces a higher net present value for a risky project
options.D: Can be applied without estimating the expected cash flows

q: Sensitivity analysis in capital budgeting is carried out in order to find out:

options.A: How the net present value (or internal rate of return) changes when one input variable, such as selling price, volume or cost, is changed while the others are held constant
options.B: The probability distribution of the net present value of the project
options.C: The optimum combination of projects to be taken up within a fixed capital budget
options.D: The sequence of decisions to be taken as the project unfolds over time
